title: Dry-run: load balancer health checks and routing
intro: About 5 minutes. The routing algorithm is the easy part — the health check is what keeps it from sending traffic into a hole.

steps.title: Round robin — simple, and wrong under uneven load
steps.explain: Round robin sends requests in a fixed rotation regardless of how busy each backend already is. It's the obvious first answer, and worth stating its failure mode immediately: a backend mid-way through a slow request still gets the next one.

steps.title: Least connections accounts for in-flight work
steps.explain: Tracking active connections per backend and routing to the least-loaded one adapts to requests that take wildly different amounts of time — the common real-world case round robin ignores.
steps.saysOutLoud: Least connections is round robin's fix for uneven request durations.

steps.title: A backend only exists in rotation if it's healthy
steps.explain: Both algorithms above assume the candidate list is already healthy backends. A background loop hits a cheap endpoint on each backend and removes it from rotation after consecutive failures — one blip shouldn't pull a backend out, but a real outage should.

steps.title: Removing a backend mid-flight still drains its requests
steps.explain: Marking a backend unhealthy stops NEW requests from routing there, but requests already in flight to it should finish rather than being cut off — that's the difference between graceful removal and an abrupt one that surfaces errors to users.

steps.title: Sticky sessions are a routing constraint, not free
steps.explain: Some apps need a user's requests to keep landing on the same backend — in-memory session state, a WebSocket. Hashing on a stable key gives that, at the cost of load balancing evenness: one backend can still end up hot if the key distribution isn't uniform.

steps.title: The load balancer itself needs to not be a single point of failure
steps.explain: A single LB instance in front of many backends just moves the single-point-of-failure problem up a layer. In practice this is solved below the application: multiple LB instances behind a floating virtual IP (keepalived/VRRP) or DNS round robin across LB nodes, so no individual load balancer process is load-bearing alone.

closing: If they push on L4 vs L7: L4 routes on IP/port with no visibility into HTTP, so it's faster but can't do path-based routing or terminate TLS — L7 costs more CPU per request but is what lets you route /api and /static to different backend pools.
